pk: a, E and O are caled vrdDi This derines the word vridhi. The leters a, E and O are vridhi leters. The sutra consists or thre words vridhi, ât and aich. at neans the long a, the rinal t being indicatory only, and is ror the sake or the pratyâhâra aich, and the pratyâhâra Ec neans the leters E and O. The indicatory t in at serves the purpose or showing that the very rorn a having two nåtrâs or prosodial neasure, is to be taken. This t also joins with the suceding vowels E and O by the rule or tapara [1.1.70] or that "which precedes or suceds t" and indicates that these vowels nust be taken as having two nâtrâs only, though they nay be the result or the conbination or vowels whose agregate nâtrâs nay be nore than two. a short vowel has one nåtrâ, a long vowel has two, and a consonant has halr a nátrâ. Thus by a rule or arn or euphonic conjunction or leters a+a=a, as naha + asaya = nahasaya. ere ha has two nâtrâs and not rour. so also KawvEqaka the vowel E the resultant or a+E has only two, not rour, nâtrâs. Thus the initial vowels in the rolowing secondary derivative nouns are vridhi rorns or their prinitive vowels. anga "bodily", ron anga; body EcCika "optional", ron icCa "option"; Opagava "the son or upagu", ron the word upagu neaning "a sage caled upagu". sinilarly in saliya "belonging to the house" the a is radical, and is also caled vridhi. The word vridhi ocurs in sûtras like sicivrdDiparasnEpadesu [7.2.1] "Let the rinal ik or the base get vridhi substitute berore the aril sic or the Parasnaipada".
ck: a, E ant O are calet vrti this terines the tort vrithi. the leters a, E ant O are vrithi leters. the sutra consists or thre torts vrithi, ât ant aich. at neans the lonk a, the rinal t peink inticatory only, ant is ror the sake or the pratyâhâra aich, ant the pratyâhâra Ec neans the leters E ant O. the inticatory t in at serves the purpose or shotink that the very rorn a havink to nåtrâs or prosotial neasure, is to pe taken. this t also coins tith the sucetink votels E ant O py the rule or tapara [1.1.70] or that "thich precetes or sucets t" ant inticates that these votels nust pe taken as havink to nâtrâs only, thoukh they nay pe the result or the conpination or votels those akrekate nâtrâs nay pe nore than to. a short votel has one nåtrâ, a lonk votel has to, ant a consonant has halr a nátrâ. thus py a rule or arn or euphonic concunction or leters a+a=a, as naha + asaya = nahasaya. ere ha has to nâtrâs ant not rour. so also katvEtaka the votel E the resultant or a+E has only to, not rour, nâtrâs. thus the initial votels in the rolotink secontary terivative nouns are vrithi rorns or their prinitive votels. anka "potily", ron anka; poty Ecika "optional", ron ica "option"; Opakava "the son or upaku", ron the tort upaku neanink "a sake calet upaku". sinilarly in saliya "pelonkink to the house" the a is ratical, ant is also calet vrithi. the tort vrithi ocurs in sûtras like sicivrtiparasnEpatesu [7.2.1] "Let the rinal ik or the pase ket vrithi supstitute perore the aril sic or the parasnaipata".
s: आ, ऐ and औ are called वृद्धि This defines the word vriddhi. The letters आ, ऐ and औ are vriddhi letters. The sutra consists of three words vriddhi, ât and aich. आत् means the long आ, the final त् being indicatory only, and is for the sake of the pratyâhâra aich, and the pratyâhâra ऐच् means the letters ऐ and औ. The indicatory त् in आत् serves the purpose of showing that the very form आ having two måtrâs or prosodial measure, is to be taken. This त् also joins with the succeeding vowels ऐ and औ by the rule of तपर [[1.1.70]] or that "which precedes or succeeds त्" and indicates that these vowels must be taken as having two mâtrâs only, though they may be the result of the combination of vowels whose aggregate mâtrâs may be more than two. A short vowel has one måtrâ, a long vowel has two, and a consonant has half a mátrâ. Thus by a rule of arm or euphonic conjunction of letters आ+आ=आ, as महा + आशयः = महाशयः. Here हा has two mâtrâs and not four. So also खट्वैडकः the vowel ऐ the resultant of आ+ऐ has only two, not four, mâtrâs. Thus the initial vowels in the following secondary derivative nouns are vriddhi forms of their primitive vowels. आङ्गः "bodily", from अङ्गः; 'body' ऐच्छिकः "optional", from इच्छा "option"; औपगवः "the son of Upagu", from the word उपगुः meaning "a sage called Upagu". Similarly in शालीयः "belonging to the house" the आ is radical, and is also called vriddhi. The word vriddhi occurs in sûtras like सिचिवृद्धिपरस्मैपदेषु [[7.2.1]] "Let the final इक् of the base get vriddhi substitute before the affix सिच् of the Parasmaipada".

pk: a, e and o are caled guna Each one or the leters a, e and o whether radical or secondary is caled a guna leter; as the initial vowels in the rolowing:- arti,"he noves"; eti "he cones", oKati "he goes." ere the initial vowels or the rots r, i, and uK have ben respectively gunated into ar, e, and o berore the third person singular ternination ti. The tern Guna ocurs in sutras like niderguna [7.3.82]. "Let there be guna substitute ror the ik or the rot nid "to nelt."
ck: a, e ant o are calet kuna Each one or the leters a, e ant o thether ratical or secontary is calet a kuna leter; as the initial votels in the rolotink:- arti,"he noves"; eti "he cones", okati "he koes." ere the initial votels or the rots r, i, ant uk have pen respectively kunatet into ar, e, ant o perore the thirt person sinkular ternination ti. the tern kuna ocurs in sutras like niterkuna [7.3.82]. "Let there pe kuna supstitute ror the ik or the rot nit "to nelt."
s: अ, ए and ओ are called गुण Each one of the letters अ, ए and ओ whether radical or secondary is called a guna letter; as the initial vowels in the following:- अर्त्ति,"he moves"; एति "he comes", ओखति "he goes." Here the initial vowels of the roots ऋ, इ, and उख् have been respectively gunated into अर्, ए, and ओ before the third person singular termination ति. The term Guna occurs in sutras like मिदेर्गुणः [[7.3.82]]. "Let there be guna substitute for the ik of the root मिद् "to melt."

pk: in the absence or any special role whenever guna or vrdDi is enjoined about any elpresion by using the terns guna or vrdDi, it is to be understod to cone in the ron or the ik (i, u, r, lr) or that elpresion. This is a paribhasha sutra, and is userul in deternining the original leters, in the place or which the substitute guna and vridhi leters wil cone. The present rule wil aply where there is the specirication or no other particular rule. Thus sutra [7.3.84] declares:- "when a sarvadhatuka or an ardhadhatuka aril rolows there is guna or the base." ere the sthani or the original elpresion which is to be gunated, is not speciried, and to conplete the sense, the word "ikah" nust be read into the sutra. The rule then being, "when a s. or an a. aril rolows there is guna or the ik vowels or the base." The guna or i or i is e; or u or u, is o, or r or r is ar, or l is al; and their Vrdhi is E, O, ar and al respectively. Thus ni + ati = ne + ati = nayati "he leads." Thererore, wherever in any rule in this Granar, guna or vridhi is ordained by enploying the terns guņa or vridhi, there the word "ikah" in the genitive case, neaning "in the place or ik", is to be suplied to conplete the sense. The word ik is thus understod in the rolowing rules, and is there qualiried by the tern anga or base:- niderguna [7.3.82] nrjervrdDi [7.2.14] pugantalaGupaDa &c., [7.3.86]; rcCatyrtan [7.4.1] rdrsoni guna [7.4.16] sTuladurayuva &c., [6.4.156]. in the rolowing sutras, the tern ik is understod and qualiries the word ånga or base, jusi ca [7.3.83], sarvaDatukarDaDatukayo [7.3.84]. These sutras wil be elplained in their proper places. The word ik has ben used in the sutra to show that the long a, ec or the diphthongs and hal or the consonants, are not to take guna or vridhi by this rule, as in the rolowing elanples yanan "a cariage", glayati "he rels aversion", unBita "conrined". ere glayati is rorned by ading the aril tip, third person singular ternination, with the clas a aril sap, to the rot glE; as glE+sap+tip=glE+a+ti. at this stage, rule [7.3.84], would require the guna substitution or the vowel or the base berore the sarvadhatuka ternination a; the guna substitute or E being e, there would be gle+ati=glayati. But this is wrong, the leter E, being not included in the pratyâhåra ik, is not arected by rule [7.3.84], and there is no guna substitution in this case. sinilarly there is no change in the long a or yanan. Thus ya+lyuw [3.3.15] = yanan [7.1.1]. ere had there ben guņa

s: In the absence of any special role whenever गुण or वृद्धि is enjoined about any expression by using the terms गुण or वृद्धि, it is to be understood to come in the room of the इक् (इ, उ, ऋ, लृ) of that expression. This is a paribhasha sutra, and is useful in determining the original letters, in the place of which the substitute guna and vriddhi letters will come. The present rule will apply where there is the specification of no other particular rule. Thus sutra [[7.3.84]] declares:- "when a sarvadhatuka or an ardhadhatuka affix follows there is guna of the base." Here the sthani or the original expression which is to be gunated, is not specified, and to complete the sense, the word "ikah" must be read into the sutra. The rule then being, "when a S. or an A. affix follows there is guna of the ik vowels of the base." The guna of इ or ई is ए; of उ or ऊ, is ओ, of ऋ or ॠ is अर्, of ऌ is अल्; and their Vrddhi is ऐ, औ, आर् and आल् respectively. Thus नी + अति = ने + अति = नयति "he leads." Therefore, wherever in any rule in this Grammar, guna or vriddhi is ordained by employing the terms guņa or vriddhi, there the word "ikah" in the genitive case, meaning "in the place of ik", is to be supplied to complete the sense. The word 'ik' is thus understood in the following rules, and is there qualified by the term अङ्ग or 'base':- मिदेर्गुणः [[7.3.82]] मृजेर्वृद्धिः [[7.2.114]] पुगन्तलघूपध &c., [[7.3.86]]; ऋच्छत्यॄताम् [[7.4.11]] ऋदृशोऽङि गुणः [[7.4.16]] स्थूलदूरयुव &c., [[6.4.156]]. In the following sutras, the term 'ik' is understood and qualifies the word ånga or base, जुसि च [[7.3.83]], सार्वधातुकार्धधातुकयोः [[7.3.84]]. These sutras will be explained in their proper places. The word 'ik' has been used in the sutra to show that the long आ, एच् or the diphthongs and हल् or the consonants, are not to take guna or vriddhi by this rule, as in the following examples यानम् "a carriage", ग्लायति "he feels aversion", उम्भिता "confined". Here ग्लायति is formed by adding the affix तिप्, third person singular termination, with the class a affix शप्, to the root ग्लै; as ग्लै+शप्+तिप्=ग्लै+अ+ति. At this stage, rule [[7.3.84]], would require the guna substitution of the vowel of the base before the sarvadhatuka termination अ; the guna substitute of ऐ being ए, there would be ग्ले+अति=ग्लयति. But this is wrong, the letter ऐ, being not included in the pratyâhåra ik, is not affected by rule [[7.3.84]], and there is no guna substitution in this case. Similarly there is no change in the long आ of यानम्. Thus या+ल्युट् [[3.3.115]] = यानम् [[7.1.1]]. Here had there been guņa by Rule [[7.3.84]], the आ of या, would have been changed into अ, and the form would have been यनम् which is wrong. But it is not so, as आ is not an इक् vowel. So also उम्भ्+इता = उम्भिता. Here, there is no guna substitution in the place of the consonant भ्. The repetition of the words guna and vriddhi in this sútra, (though by अनुवृत्ति or the supplying of a word from the previous sūtra, these words followed from the two preceding sutras) is for the purpose of indicating that, this is a restrictive rule applicable only there, where guņa or vriddhi has been ordained by the employment of the words guna or vriddhi. Therefore, it is not so in the following cases :- द्यौः "sky", पन्थाः "way" सः "he," इमम् "this". द्यौः is the nominative singular of the base दिव्. It is formed by rule [[7.1.84]], which declares that "in the nominative singular the letter औ takes the place of दिव्". Here the letter औ is no doubt a vriddhi letter, but as this substitution is not enjoined by the enunciation of the term vriddhi, औ does not take the place of the vowel इ of दिव्, but it replaces the final व्. Thus दि+औ+स्=द्यौः. Similarly rule [[7.1.85]], declares that of the word पथिन्, आ is the substitute. The आ is a vriddhi letter no doubt, but not being enunciated by the term vriddhi, it takes the place of न् of पथिन् and not of इ. Thus we have पन्थाः, the न being added by [[7.1.87]]. This is an elception to sūtra 3. By that sūtra iks were to be gunated or vridhied and by sūtra [7.3.84], the rot is to be gunated berore al ardhadhatuka terninations. al prinary ariles, that are aplied directly to rots in sanskrit, are divided into two broad clases, caled sårvadhâtuka and årdhadhâtuka. The ariles narked with an indicatory sa (caled sit), and the conjugational ariles, such as tip, ta &c., (caled tin) are sårvadhatuka; al other ariles are caled årdhadhâtuka. Though by the general rule, [7.3.84], the rot is to be gunated berore årdhadhâtuka terninations, yet it is not to be so, berore those ariles which cause the lopa loping or or elipses or a portion or a nenber or the original dhấtu. Thus the ternination syani is a rirst person singular ternination or the ruture tense ( lrw ) and is an ardhadhâtuka ternination; when this is aded to rot ji to elcel the i or ji becones gunated and we have jesyani "i shal or wil elcel." But in those cases where there is a lopa or the nenber or a rot rorn, caused by an aril, there is no guṇation. Thus in loluva "a great cuter", the original rot is lu "to cut" which rorns the intensive verb loluya. in rorning the noun or agency ron the verb loluya, an ardhadhatuka suril ac [3.1.134], is aded. Thus loluya+ac. at this stage, by rorce or sūtra [2.4.74] which declares that "berore the aril ac [3.1.134] the ya or the intensive verb nust be supresed," the ya is droped and we have lolu+a. ere by the general rule [7.3.84], the rinal u would have ben gunated. But by virtue or the present sūtra, no guna takes place, because here on acount or the ardhadhâtuka aril ac, a portion or the rot, nanely, ya, has ben elided; thererore no guņa takes place. Thus we have loluva "a great cuter." s: The गुण and वृद्धि substitutions which otherwise would have presented themselves do not take place, when such an आर्धधातुक [[3.4.114]] affix follows, which causes a portion of the root to be elided. This is an exception to sūtra 3. By that sūtra iks were to be gunated or vriddhied and by sūtra [[7.3.84]], the root is to be gunated before all ardhadhatuka terminations. All primary affixes, that are applied directly to roots in Sanskrit, are divided into two broad classes, called sårvadhâtuka and årdhadhâtuka. The affixes marked with an indicatory श (called शित्), and the conjugational affixes, such as तिप्, तः &c., (called तिङ्) are sårvadhatuka; all other affixes are called årdhadhâtuka. Though by the general rule, [[7.3.84]], the root is to be gunated before årdhadhâtuka terminations, yet it is not to be so, before those affixes which cause the लोप 'lopping off or ellipses' of a portion or a member of the original dhấtu. Thus the termination स्यामि is a first person singular termination of the future tense ( लृट् ) and is an ardhadhâtuka termination; when this is added to root जि 'to excel' the इ of जि becomes gunated and we have जेष्यामि "I shall or will excel." But in those cases where there is a lopa of the member of a root form, caused by an affix, there is no guṇation. Thus in लोलुवः "a great cutter", the original root is लू "to cut" which forms the Intensive verb लोलूय. In forming the noun of agency from the verb लोलूय, an ardhadhatuka suffix अच् [[3.1.134]], is added. Thus लोलूय+अच्. At this stage, by force of sūtra [[2.4.74]] which declares that "before the affix अच् [[3.1.134]] the य of the Intensive verb must be suppressed," the ya is dropped and we have लोलू+अ. Here by the general rule [[7.3.84]], the final ऊ would have been gunated. But by virtue of the present sūtra, no guna takes place, because here on account of the ardhadhâtuka affix अच्, a portion of the root, namely, य, has been elided; therefore no guņa takes place. Thus we have लोलुवः "a great cutter." The word धातु "root" has been used in the sûtra, in order to indicate that the exception does not apply where there is an elision of an anubandha or of an affix. As in लूञ्+इता = लो+इता = लविता. Here the indicatory letter ञ् has been elided, but that does not prevent gunation. Similarly in रेड् the affix विच् is added to the root रिष् "to injure." Thus रिष्+विच् [[3.2.75]] = रिष्+व् [[1.3.2]] and [[1.3.3]] = रिष्+० [[6.1.67]]. Here the affix व् is elided, but nevertheless, the guṇa substitute must take place in रिष्. Thus we have रिष्+० = रेष् [[7.3.86]] and [[1.1.62]] = रेड् [[8.2.39]]. The word ardhadhâtuka has been used to indicate that a sarvadhatuka affix which causes the elision of a portion of a root, does not prevent guna or vriddhi as in रोरवीति, (Rig Veda IV.58.3) "he roars much". रू+यङ् = रोरुव [[3.1.22]]. रोरुय+तिप् = रोरु+ति [[2.4.74]]. Here the sarvadhatuka affix तिप् causes the elision of य, a portion of the root. The guna substitution however takes place, and we have रोरो+ई+ति [[7.3.94]] = रोरवीति, the augment ईट् being added by sūtra [[7.3.94]]. The word "ikah" of the previous sūtra is understood in this sūtra also. The ik letters only are not gunated or vriddhied before such ardhadbatuka affixes; the other vowels may do so. Thus in अभाजि the equation is as follows:- अ+भञ्ज्+चिण् = अ+भज्+इ [[6.4.33]]. Here the ardhadhátuka affix चिण् has caused a portion of the root भञ्ज्, to be suppressed, vis., the letter ञ् has been elided. But nevertheless the अ of भज् is vriddhied before चिण् because अ is not included in the pratyahara ik ; and the exception contained in the present sutra only applies to the ik letters. So also रञ्ज्+घञ् [[3.3.18]] = रज्+अ [[6.4.27]] = रागः [[7.2.116]] and [[7.3.52]].

pk: and that, which otherwise would have caused guna or vrdDi, does not do so, when it has an indicatory k , g , n Thus the past participle terninations kta and ktavatu are ardhadhatuka ariles, which would, by the general rule [7.3.84], have caused guna, but as their indicatory leter ka is it, the real terninations being, ta and tavat, they do not cause guna. Thererore, when these terninations are aded to a rot, the ik or the rot is not gunated. Thus with the rot ci "to colect" we have cita or citavan, sru, "to hear", sruta, srutavan; Bi; "to rear" Bita, Bitavan. sinilarly the terninations kyap kelina, kvasu kanac, ktva, ktin, &c., are al kit terninations the indicatory leters or al being k, the real ariles being ya, elin, vas &c. &c. &c. Berore these, the rot is not gunated. Thus we have ron Br "to bear" Brtva, ron Bid "to pierce" Bidelina. The terns kit &c., or this sûtra are in the locative or seventh case. The rorce or this case ternination here is that or ninita or cause, that is the guna or vridhi which would otherwise have ben caused, does not take place, ir an aril is kit, git, nit. Thus al ardhadhâtuka and sårvadhatuka ariles cause gunation or the rinal ik or the inrlective base [7.3.84] Thus the sårvadhâtuka aril sap(a) in the rolowing:- Bu+sap+tip = Bo+a+ti = Bavati "he is." sinilarly sårvadhatuka and ardbadhâtuka ariles cause the guna substitution or the short penultinate ik or the inrlective base [7.3.85]. Thus buD+sap+tip = boDati. The general rorce or the locative case in an aphorisn is to cause the operation directed, on the elpresion inediately preceding it [1.1.6]. ir the rorce or the locative case in the present sūtra were also that as elplained in [1.1.6], then the interpretation would be this:- an aril having an indicatory k, g or ṅ, would not cause the guna substitution or the vowel ik, inediately preceding it. The case or the penultinate short ik wil not be covered by it. Then though the rule nay aply to ci+kta=cita "colected" it would not aply to Bid+kta; there would be nothing to bar the guna substitution or the penultinate i or Bid. This however is prevented by elplaining the locative as one or "ocasion" and thus Bid+kta = Bina "broken." sinilarly ron the rot ji we have a word jisnu victorious, in which the aril gsnu has an indicatory g. Thus ji+gsnu = jisnu "victorious" [3.2.139], so also sTasnu "durable," sinilarly the aril, an is a nit aril, the real suril being a, the n being nerely indicatory. Thererore when an is aded to a rot,

s: And that, which otherwise would have caused गुण or वृद्धि, does not do so, when it has an indicatory क् , ग् , ङ् Thus the past participle terminations क्त and क्तवतु are ardhadhatuka affixes, which would, by the general rule [[7.3.84]], have caused guna, but as their indicatory letter क is इत्, the real terminations being, त and तवत्, they do not cause guna. Therefore, when these terminations are added to a root, the ik of the root is not gunated. Thus with the root चि "to collect" we have चितः or चितवान्, श्रू, "to hear", श्रुतः, श्रुतवान्; भी; "to fear" भीतः, भीतवान्. Similarly the terminations क्यप् केलिम, क्वसु कानच्, क्त्वा, क्तिन्, &c., are all कित् terminations 'the indicatory letters of all being क्,' the real affixes being य, एलिम्, वस् &c. &c. &c. Before these, the root is not gunated. Thus we have from भृ "to bear" भृत्व, from भिद् "to pierce" भिदेलिम. The terms कित् &c., of this sûtra are in the locative or seventh case. The force of this case termination here is that of निमित or cause, that is the guna or vriddhi which would otherwise have been caused, does not take place, if an affix is कित्, गित्, ङित्. Thus all ardhadhâtuka and sårvadhatuka affixes cause gunation of the final ik of the inflective base [[7.3.84]] Thus the Sårvadhâtuka affix शप्(अ) in the following:- भू+शप्+तिप् = भो+अ+ति = भवति "he is." Similarly sårvadhatuka and ardbadhâtuka affixes cause the guna substitution of the short penultimate ik of the inflective base [[7.3.85]]. Thus बुध्+शप्+तिप् = बोधति. The general force of the locative case in an aphorism is to cause the operation directed, on the expression immediately preceding it [[1.1.66]]. If the force of the locative case in the present sūtra were also that as explained in [[1.1.66]], then the interpretation would be this:- An affix having an indicatory k, g or ṅ, would not cause the guna substitution of the vowel ik, immediately preceding it. The case of the penultimate short ik will not be covered by it. Then though the rule may apply to चि+क्त=चितः "collected" it would not apply to भिद्+क्त; there would be nothing to bar the guna substitution of the penultimate इ of भिद्. This however is prevented by explaining the locative as one of "occasion" and thus भिद्+क्त = भिन्नः "broken." Similarly from the root जि we have a word जिष्णुः 'victorious', in which the affix ग्स्नु has an indicatory ग्. Thus जि+ग्स्नु = जिष्णुः "victorious" [[3.2.139]], so also स्थास्नुः "durable," Similarly the affix, अङ् is a ङित् affix, the real suffix being अ, the ङ् being merely indicatory. Therefore when अङ् is added to a root, there is no gunation or vriddhing. Thus we have from विद् "to know" विदः. Similarly by [[1.2.4]], all sårvadhâtuka affixes that are not marked by an indicatory प्, are treated as ङित्. Thus the second person singular termination तस् is ङित्, and we have चिनुतः "they two collect," similarly चिन्वन्ति, "they collect", मृज्+क्त = मृष्टः "cleansed," मृजन्ति "they cleanse." The phrase "when indicated by the term ik" is understood in this sutra. The prohibition, therefore, applies to ik vowels only, and not to all vowels in general. Thus by [[3.1.30]], the root कम् "to desire" takes the affix णिङ्; of this affix the letters ण् and ङ् are indicatory, the real affix is इ. The force of ण् is to cause vriddhi [[7.2.116]]. The indicatory ङ् does not prevent such vriddhi, as the letter अ of कम् is not included in ik. Thus we have कामि+अते = कामे+अते = कामयते "he desires". According to the wish of the author of the Mahabhashya, the verb मृज् optionally takes vriddhi, before kit or ṅit affixes beginning with a vowel. As परिमृजन्ति or परिमार्जन्ति "they rub." Here in this sūtra there is prohibition of the guna of the short penultimate ik also. The indicatory ङ् of the verbal tense affixes i.e., लङ्, लिङ्, लुङ्, लृङ् is an exception to this rule of ङित्. This is an inference deduced from [[3.4.104]] which declares "when the sense is that of benediction, then the augment यासुट् of लिङ् is as if it were d

pk: The guna and vrdDi substitutions which otherwise would have presented thenselves do not however cone, in the place or the vowels or diDi to shine and vevi to go, and or the augnent caled iw The rots diDi and vevi never take the guna or vridhi substitutions under ordinary circunstances. Thus the aril nvul generaly causes vridhi substitution when aded to any rot; and so the aril lyuw causes guņa. But these ariles when aplied to the verbs didhi and vevi, never cause vřidhi or guna substitution. as adiDi+nvul = adiDi+aka [7.1.1] = adiDvaka [6.1.7]. so also adiDi+lyuw = adiDi+ana [7.1.1] = adiDvanan. sinilarly ron vevi we have avevyanan and avevyaka. in the Vedas, however, these verbs take guna. Thus adiDet (nig Ved. l.98.7), and adiDayu (nig Ved. V.40.5). These two verbs are conrined generaly to the Vedic literature, and the present rule thererore, sens to be an unecesary prohibition; as they take guna in spite or such prohibition. Or the augnent iw the real aril is i. in the general tenses, it is aded to certain terninations begining with consonants or the val clas, i.e., al consonants elcept ya [7.2.35]. Thus the ruture ternination, rirst person, singular is syani; this when aded to the rot car "to nove" requires an internediate i, and thus we have the rorn carisyani, i shal walk. This i is never gunated or vridhied, though acording to the general rule, coning berore an ardhadhâtuka ternination, it ought to have ben gunated. The augnent iw, could under no circunstances have taken vridhi, the prohibition thererore, is in the case or the guna substitute or iw.
ck: the kuna ant vrti supstitutions thich othertise toult have presentet thenselves to not hotever cone, in the place or the votels or titi to shine ant vevi to ko, ant or the auknent calet it the rots titi ant vevi never take the kuna or vrithi supstitutions unter ortinary circunstances. thus the aril nvul keneraly causes vrithi supstitution then atet to any rot; ant so the aril lyut causes kuņa. put these ariles then apliet to the verps tithi ant vevi, never cause vřithi or kuna supstitution. as atiti+nvul = atiti+aka [7.1.1] = atitvaka [6.1.7]. so also atiti+lyut = atiti+ana [7.1.1] = atitvanan. sinilarly ron vevi te have avevyanan ant avevyaka. in the Vetas, hotever, these verps take kuna. thus atitet (nik Vet. l.98.7), ant atitayu (nik Vet. V.40.5). these to verps are conrinet keneraly to the Vetic literature, ant the present rule thererore, sens to pe an unecesary prohipition; as they take kuna in spite or such prohipition. Or the auknent it the real aril is i. in the keneral tenses, it is atet to certain terninations pekinink tith consonants or the val clas, i.e., al consonants elcept ya [7.2.35]. thus the ruture ternination, rirst person, sinkular is syani; this then atet to the rot car "to nove" retuires an internetiate i, ant thus te have the rorn carisyani, i shal talk. this i is never kunatet or vrithiet, thoukh acortink to the keneral rule, conink perore an arthathâtuka ternination, it oukht to have pen kunatet. the auknent it, coult unter no circunstances have taken vrithi, the prohipition thererore, is in the case or the kuna supstitute or it.
s: The गुण and वृद्धि substitutions which otherwise would have presented themselves do not however come, in the place of the vowels of दिधि 'to shine' and वेवि 'to go', and of the augment called इट् The roots दीधी and वेवी never take the guna or vriddhi substitutions under ordinary circumstances. Thus the affix ण्वुल् generally causes vriddhi substitution when added to any root; and so the affix ल्युट् causes guņa. But these affixes when applied to the verbs didhi and vevi, never cause vřiddhi or guna substitution. As आदीधी+ण्वुल् = आदीधी+अक [[7.1.1]] = आदीध्वकः [[6.1.77]]. So also आदीधी+ल्युट् = आदीधी+अन [[7.1.1]] = आदीध्वनम्. Similarly from वेवी we have आवेव्यनम् and आवेव्यकः. In the Vedas, however, these verbs take guna. Thus अदीधेत् (Rig Ved. X.98.7), and अदीधयुः (Rig Ved. V.40.5). These two verbs are confined generally to the Vedic literature, and the present rule therefore, seems to be an unnecessary prohibition; as they take guna in spite of such prohibition. Of the augment इट् the real affix is इ. In the general tenses, it is added to certain terminations beginning with consonants of the वल् class, i.e., all consonants except य [[7.2.35]]. Thus the future termination, first person, singular is स्यामि; this when added to the root चर् "to move" requires an intermediate इ, and thus we have the form चरिष्यामि, 'I shall walk.' This इ is never gunated or vriddhied, though according to the general rule, coming before an ardhadhâtuka termination, it ought to have been gunated. The augment इट्, could under no circumstances have taken vriddhi, the prohibition therefore, is in the case of the guna substitute of इट्.

pk: Consonants unseparated by a vowel are caled conjunct consonants. This derines the word sanyoga. The sûtra consists or thre words, hala, the plural or the pratyåhåra hal, denoting al the consonants, anantara neans "without any separation or space" and sanyoga which is the word derined, and neans "conjunct consonants." so that the sūtra neans, conjunct consonants are those consonants betwen which there is no heterogeneous separating vowel and which are pronounced jointly, such as ka in the word kukuwa, "cock." The word "sanyoga" aplies to the whole or the conjunct consonants jointly and not to then separately. The plural nunber shows that the conjunction nay be or two or nore consonants. Why do we say "consonant"? ir two vowels cone together they wil not be caled "sanyoga". Thus titaucCatran "a sieve unbrela", the two vowels a and u have cone together unseparated by any consonant; yet they are not caled sanyoga, otherwise the rinal u would have ben rejected by [8.2.23] "there is elision or the rinal or that pada which ends in a sanyoga leter." Why do we say "unseparated by a vowel"? ir consonants separated by a vowel were also caled sanyoga, then in the sentence pacati panasan, the sylable san would be caled sanyoga, and by [8.2.29], the initial sa would be elided.
ck: consonants unseparatet py a votel are calet concunct consonants. this terines the tort sanyoka. the sûtra consists or thre torts, hala, the plural or the pratyåhåra hal, tenotink al the consonants, anantara neans "tithout any separation or space" ant sanyoka thich is the tort terinet, ant neans "concunct consonants." so that the sūtra neans, concunct consonants are those consonants peten thich there is no heterokeneous separatink votel ant thich are pronouncet cointly, such as ka in the tort kukuta, "cock." the tort "sanyoka" aplies to the thole or the concunct consonants cointly ant not to then separately. the plural nunper shots that the concunction nay pe or to or nore consonants. thy to te say "consonant"? ir to votels cone tokether they til not pe calet "sanyoka". thus titaucatran "a sieve unprela", the to votels a ant u have cone tokether unseparatet py any consonant; yet they are not calet sanyoka, othertise the rinal u toult have pen recectet py [8.2.23] "there is elision or the rinal or that pata thich ents in a sanyoka leter." thy to te say "unseparatet py a votel"? ir consonants separatet py a votel tere also calet sanyoka, then in the sentence pacati panasan, the sylaple san toult pe calet sanyoka, ant py [8.2.29], the initial sa toult pe elitet.
s: Consonants unseparated by a vowel are called conjunct consonants. This defines the word sanyoga. The sûtra consists of three words, हलः, the plural of the pratyåhåra हल्, denoting all the consonants, अनन्तरः means "without any separation or space" and संयोगः which is the word defined, and means "conjunct consonants." So that the sūtra means, conjunct consonants are those consonants between which there is no heterogeneous separating vowel and which are pronounced jointly, such as क्क in the word कुक्कुटः, "cock." The word "sanyoga" applies to the whole of the conjunct consonants jointly and not to them separately. The plural number shows that the conjunction may be of two or more consonants. Why do we say "consonant"? If two vowels come together they will not be called "sanyoga". Thus तितउच्छत्रं "a sieve umbrella", the two vowels अ and उ have come together unseparated by any consonant; yet they are not called sanyoga, otherwise the final उ would have been rejected by [[8.2.23]] "there is elision of the final of that pada which ends in a sanyoga letter." Why do we say "unseparated by a vowel"? If consonants separated by a vowel were also called sanyoga, then in the sentence पचति पनसम्, the syllable सम् would be called sanyoga, and by [[8.2.29]], the initial स would be elided.

pk: That which is pronounced by the nose along with the nouth is caled anunasika or nasal. This derines the word anunåsika. The sûtra consists or rour words nuKa "nouth" nasika "nose" vacana "uterance or pronunciation" and anunasika "nasals." Though the words nuKa + nasika [2.4.2] wil by the rule or conposition rorn nuKanasikan and not nuKanasika, yet the later rorn night be held to be an iregularity; or the phrase nuKanasikavacanan nay be regarded as a conpound or nuKanasika+avacanan, the word avachana neaning "partial uterance." That is a leter partialy utered by the nose and partialy by the nouth would be caled anunåsika. Thererore the nasals are those leters which are pronounced ron two organs or places, i.e., the nouth and the nose. The pure nasal is anusvåra, while anunasikas are direrent ron this, in as nuch as, that in pronouncing these, the breath pases through the nose and the nouth. The vowels are generaly so nasalised. ir, instead or eniting the vowel sound rely through the nouth, we alow the velun pendulun to drop and the air to vibrate through the cavities which conect the nose with the pharynl, we hear the nasal vowels (anunåsika). Thus an, an. in the Vedas, the particle an is anunåsika. as aBra an apa (nig Veda. V.48.1), so also parsi dine gaBira an ugraputre (nig Ved. Vi.67.1). The consonants na, na, na, na and na are also anunåsika. Thus na is pronounced by the throat along with the nose, na by the palate and nose, na by the uper palate and nose; na by the teth and nose, and na by the lip and nose. The seni-vowels ya, na and la are also nasalised and are then caled anunåsika. The tern anunåsika is used in sūtra [5.1.126] &c. Why have we used the word "by the nouth"? This derinition wil not include anusvåra or the pure nasal, which is pronounced wholy through the nose. Why have we used the word "by the nose"? in order to elclude the consonants ka, ca, wa, ta, pa &c. &c., which are pronounced wholy and solely through the nouth.
ck: that thich is pronouncet py the nose alonk tith the nouth is calet anunasika or nasal. this terines the tort anunåsika. the sûtra consists or rour torts nuka "nouth" nasika "nose" vacana "uterance or pronunciation" ant anunasika "nasals." thoukh the torts nuka + nasika [2.4.2] til py the rule or conposition rorn nukanasikan ant not nukanasika, yet the later rorn nikht pe helt to pe an irekularity; or the phrase nukanasikavacanan nay pe rekartet as a conpount or nukanasika+avacanan, the tort avachana neanink "partial uterance." that is a leter partialy uteret py the nose ant partialy py the nouth toult pe calet anunåsika. thererore the nasals are those leters thich are pronouncet ron to orkans or places, i.e., the nouth ant the nose. the pure nasal is anusvåra, thile anunasikas are tirerent ron this, in as nuch as, that in pronouncink these, the preath pases throukh the nose ant the nouth. the votels are keneraly so nasaliset. ir, insteat or enitink the votel sount rely throukh the nouth, te alot the velun pentulun to trop ant the air to viprate throukh the cavities thich conect the nose tith the pharynl, te hear the nasal votels (anunåsika). thus an, an. in the Vetas, the particle an is anunåsika. as apra an apa (nik Veta. V.48.1), so also parsi tine kapira an ukraputre (nik Vet. Vi.67.1). the consonants na, na, na, na ant na are also anunåsika. thus na is pronouncet py the throat alonk tith the nose, na py the palate ant nose, na py the uper palate ant nose; na py the teth ant nose, ant na py the lip ant nose. the seni-votels ya, na ant la are also nasaliset ant are then calet anunåsika. the tern anunåsika is uset in sūtra [5.1.126] &c. thy have te uset the tort "py the nouth"? this terinition til not inclute anusvåra or the pure nasal, thich is pronouncet tholy throukh the nose. thy have te uset the tort "py the nose"? in orter to elclute the consonants ka, ca, ta, ta, pa &c. &c., thich are pronouncet tholy ant solely throukh the nouth.
s: That which is pronounced by the nose along with the mouth is called अनुनासिक or nasal. This defines the word anunåsika. The sûtra consists of four words मुख "mouth" नासिका "nose" वचनः "utterance or pronunciation" and अनुनासिकः "nasals." Though the words मुख + नासिका [[2.4.2]] will by the rule of composition form मुखनासिकं and not मुखनासिका, yet the latter form might be held to be an irregularity; or the phrase मुखनासिकावचनं may be regarded as a compound of मुखनासिक+आवचनं, the word avachana meaning "partial utterance." That is a letter partially uttered by the nose and partially by the mouth would be called anunåsika. Therefore the nasals are those letters which are pronounced from two organs or places, i.e., the mouth and the nose. The pure nasal is anusvåra, while anunasikas are different from this, in as much as, that in pronouncing these, the breath passes through the nose and the mouth. The vowels are generally so nasalised. 'If, instead of emitting the vowel sound freely through the mouth, we allow the velum pendulum to drop and the air to vibrate through the cavities which connect the nose with the pharynx, we hear the nasal vowels (anunåsika).' Thus अँ, आँ. In the Vedas, the particle आङ् is anunåsika. As अभ्र आँ अपः (Rig Veda. V.48.1), so also पर्षि दीने गभीर आँ उग्रपुत्रे (Rig Ved. VIII.67.11). The consonants ङ, ञ, ण, न and म are also anunåsika. Thus ङ is pronounced by the throat along with the nose, ञ by the palate and nose, ण by the upper palate and nose; न by the teeth and nose, and म by the lip and nose. The semi-vowels य, न and ल are also nasalised and are then called anunåsika. The term anunåsika is used in sūtra [[5.1.126]] &c. Why have we used the word "by the mouth"? This definition will not include anusvåra or the pure nasal, which is pronounced wholly through the nose. Why have we used the word "by the nose"? In order to exclude the consonants क, च, ट, त, प &c. &c., which are pronounced wholly and solely through the mouth.

pk: Those whose place or uterance and erort are equal are caled savarna or honogeneous leters. This derines the word savarna or a honogeneous leter. The sūtra consists or rour words :- tulya "equal or sinilar," asya "nouth or place or pronunciation," prayatna "erort" and savarnan "words or the sane clas." The asya or places or portions or the nouth by contact with which various sounds are rorned are chierly the rolowing :- 1. kanWa "throat" 2. talu palate, 3. nurdDa, head, 4. danta teth, 5. osWO lips, 6. nasika nose. The prayatnan or quality or erort is or two sorts prinarily, aByantara "internal" and bahya "elternal." The rirst is again sub-divided into rive parts:- 1. sprswan or conplete contact or the organs. The twenty-rive leters ron ka to na belong to this clas. in pronouncing these there is a conplete contact or the rot or the tongue with the various places, such as throat, palate, done or the palate, teth and lip. 2. isatsprswan or slight contact. The leters ya, ra, la, va belong to this clas or contacts. "in pronouncing these seni-vowels the two organs, the active and pasive, which are necesary ror the production or al consonantal noises, are not alowed to touch each other, but only to aproach." 3. vivrtan or conplete opening. The vowels belong to this clas. 4. isad vivrtan or slight opening. The leters sa, sa, sa, ha belong to this clas. sone however place the vowels and sa &c., into one group and cal then al vivrita. 5. sanvrtan or contracted. in actual use, the organ in the enunciation or the short a is contracted but it is considered to be open only, as in the case or the other vowels, when the vowel a is in the state or taking part in sone operation or granar. The abhyantara prayatna is the node or articulation preparatory to the uterance or the sound, the båhya-prayatna is the node or articulation at the close or the uterance or the sound. The division or leters acording to abhyantra prayatna has ben already given. By that we get, 1. the sparsa or nute leters, 2. the antastha or internediate betwen sparsas and ushnans, or seni-vowel or liquid leters, 3. the svaras or vowels or vivrita leters, 4. the ushnans or sibilants or rlatus leters. The division or leters acording to båhya prayatna gives us rirst surds or aghosha leters, 2. sonants or ghosha leters. The aghosha are also caled svasa leters, the ghoshas are caled nåda leters. The second division or leters acording to båhya prayatna is into; 1. aspirated (nahåprana). 2. unaspirated

s: Those whose place of utterance and effort are equal are called सवर्ण or homogeneous letters. This defines the word savarna or a homogeneous letter. The sūtra consists of four words :- तुल्य "equal or similar," आस्य "mouth or place of pronunciation," प्रयत्न "effort" and सवर्णम् "words of the same class." The आस्य or places or portions of the mouth by contact with which various sounds are formed are chiefly the following :- 1. कण्ठ "throat" 2. तालु 'palate,' 3. मूर्द्धा, 'head,' 4. दन्ताः 'teeth,' 5. ओष्ठौ 'lips,' 6. नासिका 'nose.' The प्रयत्नम् or quality or effort is of two sorts primarily, आभ्यन्तरः "internal" and बाह्यः "external." The first is again sub-divided into five parts:- 1. स्पृष्टम् or complete contact of the organs. The twenty-five letters from क to म belong to this class. In pronouncing these there is a complete contact of the root of the tongue with the various places, such as throat, palate, dome of the palate, teeth and lip. 2. ईषत्स्पृष्टम् or slight contact. The letters य, र, ल, व belong to this class of contacts. "In pronouncing these semi-vowels the two organs, the active and passive, which are necessary for the production of all consonantal noises, are not allowed to touch each other, but only to approach." 3. विवृतम् or complete opening. The vowels belong to this class. 4. ईषद् विवृतम् or slight opening. The letters श, ष, स, ह belong to this class. Some however place the vowels and श &c., into one group and call them all vivrita. 5. संवृतम् or contracted. In actual use, the organ in the enunciation of the short अ is contracted but it is considered to be open only, as in the case of the other vowels, when the vowel अ is in the state of taking part in some operation of grammar. The abhyantara prayatna is the mode of articulation preparatory to the utterance of the sound, the båhya-prayatna is the mode of articulation at the close of the utterance of the sound. The division of letters according to abhyantra prayatna has been already given. By that we get, 1. the sparsa or mute letters, 2. the antastha or intermediate between sparsas and ushmans, or semi-vowel or liquid letters, 3. the svaras or vowels or vivrita letters, 4. the ushmans or sibilants or flatus letters. The division of letters according to båhya prayatna gives us first surds or aghosha letters, 2. sonants or ghosha letters. The aghosha are also called svasa letters, the ghoshas are called nåda letters. The second division of letters according to båhya prayatna is into; 1. Aspirated (mahåprana). 2. Unaspirated (alpaprana). The vowel अ has eighteen forms. The acute अ (udatta), grave अ (anudatta) and circumflexed अ ( svarita). Each one of these three may be nasalised (anunasika), or not (niranunasika). Then lastly everyone of these six may be short, long, or prolated. Thus:- अ, अ, अ, अँ, अँ, अँ, आ, आ, आ, आँ, आँ, आँ, अ३, अ३, अ३, अँ३, अँ३, अँ३. Similarly the letters इ, उ and ऋ have also eighteen forms. The letter ऌ has no long form; it has therefore 12 modifications. The diphthongs have no short forms, they have therefore, only 12 forms. The antastha or semi-vowels with the exception of र have two forms each vis., nasalised and un-nasalised. The semi-vowels have no homogeneous letters corresponding to them. All letters of a varga or 'class' are homogeneous to each other. Thus then the homogeneous or savarna letters must satisfy two conditions before they could be called savarna. First, their place of pronunciation or आस्य must be the same. Secondly their प्रयत्न or quality must be equal. If one condition be present and the other be absent, there can be no savarna-hood. Thus च and श are both palatals, their आस्य or place of pronunciation being तालु 'palate', but still they are not savarna, because their प्रयत्न is different, the प्रयत्न of च being sprishta and that of श being vivrita. Similarly क and च though their प्रयत्न is the same i.e., sprishta, yet their आस्य being different, one being guttural and the other palatal, are not savarna. There is

pk: There is however no honogeneity betwen vowels and consonants, though their place and erort be equal. This sutra lays down an elception to the rorner sutra. There can be no honogeneity or savarna relationship betwen vowels and consonants, though their asya and prayatna nay be the sane. Thus i and sa have the sane asya nanely talu palate, and the sane prayatna nanely vivrita, but stil they are not to be caled savarna. Thus in danqahasta, daDisitalan &c., the leters a and ha in the rirst elanple, and i and sa in the second not being honogeneous leters; there is no conbination or sandhi, which would otherwise have taken place. sinilarly ir sa and i be held honogeneous, then vipasa+an [4.3.53] = vipas+an [6.4.148]; here sa would be elided by [6.4.148], but it is not so and we have vEpasa "belonging to vipåså or born therein." so also in anaquhan "ol-skin," the ha would have ben onited, ir held honogeneous with a.
ck: there is hotever no honokeneity peten votels ant consonants, thoukh their place ant erort pe etual. this sutra lays totn an elception to the rorner sutra. there can pe no honokeneity or savarna relationship peten votels ant consonants, thoukh their asya ant prayatna nay pe the sane. thus i ant sa have the sane asya nanely talu palate, ant the sane prayatna nanely vivrita, put stil they are not to pe calet savarna. thus in tantahasta, tatisitalan &c., the leters a ant ha in the rirst elanple, ant i ant sa in the secont not peink honokeneous leters; there is no conpination or santhi, thich toult othertise have taken place. sinilarly ir sa ant i pe helt honokeneous, then vipasa+an [4.3.53] = vipas+an [6.4.148]; here sa toult pe elitet py [6.4.148], put it is not so ant te have vEpasa "pelonkink to vipåså or porn therein." so also in anatuhan "ol-skin," the ha toult have pen onitet, ir helt honokeneous tith a.
s: There is however no homogeneity between vowels and consonants, though their place and effort be equal. This sutra lays down an exception to the former sutra. There can be no homogeneity or savarna relationship between vowels and consonants, though their आस्य and प्रयत्न may be the same. Thus इ and श have the same आस्य namely तालु 'palate,' and the same प्रयत्नः namely vivrita, but still they are not to be called savarna. Thus in दण्डहस्त, दधिशीतलं &c., the letters अ and ह in the first example, and इ and श in the second not being homogeneous letters; there is no combination or sandhi, which would otherwise have taken place. Similarly if श and इ be held homogeneous, then विपाश+अण् [[4.3.53]] = विपाश्+अण् [[6.4.148]]; here श would be elided by [[6.4.148]], but it is not so and we have वैपाशः "belonging to vipåså or born therein." So also in आनडुहं "ox-skin," the ह would have been omitted, if held homogeneous with अ.

pk: a dual case aril ending in i or u or e is caled pragrhya , or elcepted vowels which do not adnit sanDi or conjugation. as a general rule, sanskrit alows or no hiatus in a sentence. ir a word ends in a vowel, and the nelt word begins with a vowel, the two vowels coalesce, acording to certain rules. This is caled sandhi. But pragrihyas are elceptions to this sandhi, "they are certain terninations, the rinal vowels or which are not liable to any sandhi rules." [6.1.125]. This sutra gives thre or these terninations, vis., the duals or nouns or verbs ending in i (it), u (ut), e (et). Thus:- kavi inO "these two poets," so also vayu iti "two winds;" nale iti "these two garlands." pacete iti "they two cok" paceTe iti "you two cok." ere acording to the general rule or sandhi, the rinal i or kavi and the initial i or inO ought to have coalesced into an i, but it is not so, because kavi is the noninative dual or kavi. Why do we say ending in ī, ū and e? Because when the dual ends in any other vowel this rule wil not aply. as vrksO+atra = vrksavatra, "these two tres" [6.1.78]. Or course it rolows ron the derinition, that i, u, or e or the dual nunber only are pragrihya; ir these vowels terninate any other nunber they wil not be pragřihya but wil rolow the general rule or sandhi, as kunari (i.s.) + atra = kunaryatra, "the girl is here" [6.1.7]. Vart: The prohibition or naniva &c., should be stated in treating or the pragrihya nature or i, u &c. Thus nani (two gens) + iva = naniva "like two gens". so also danpativa "like a couple," janpativa "like nan and wire," rodasiva "like heaven and earth." sone say that this vårtika is unecesary. Because the rinal nenber or the above words is not iva, but the particle va only; which has the sane neaning as iva.

s: A dual case affix ending in ई or ऊ or ए is called प्रगृह्य , or excepted vowels which do not admit सन्धि or conjugation. As a general rule, Sanskrit allows of no hiatus in a sentence. If a word ends in a vowel, and the next word begins with a vowel, the two vowels coalesce, according to certain rules. This is called sandhi. But pragrihyas are exceptions to this sandhi, "they are certain terminations, the final vowels of which are not liable to any sandhi rules." [[6.1.125]]. This sutra gives three of these terminations, viz., the duals of nouns or verbs ending in ई (ईत्), ऊ (ऊत्), ए (एत्). Thus:- कवी इमौ "these two poets," so also वायू इति "two winds;" माले इति "these two garlands." पचेते इति "they two cook" पचेथे इति "you two cook." Here according to the general rule of sandhi, the final इ of कवी and the initial इ of इमौ ought to have coalesced into an ई, but it is not so, because कवी is the nominative dual of कवि. Why do we say ending in ī, ū and e? Because when the dual ends in any other vowel this rule will not apply. As वृक्षौ+अत्र = वृक्षावत्र, "these two trees" [[6.1.78]]. Of course it follows from the definition, that ई, ऊ, or ए of the dual number only are pragrihya; if these vowels terminate any other number they will not be pragřihya but will follow the general rule of sandhi, as कुमारी (I.S.) + अत्र = कुमार्य्यत्र, "the girl is here" [[6.1.77]]. Vart: The prohibition of मनीव &c., should be stated in treating of the pragrihya nature of ई, ऊ &c. Thus मनी (two gems) + इव = मनीव "like two gems". So also दम्पतीव "like a couple," जम्पतीव "like man and wife," रोदसीव "like heaven and earth." Some say that this vårtika is unneccessary. Because the final member of the above words is not इव, but the particle व only; which has the same meaning as iva.

pk: The sane leters arter the n or the pronoun adas are pragrhya in the pronoun adas, the dual ternination in i, u or e wil be pragrihya by rorce or the last sūtra, but the present sûtra nakes this adition, that in the case or adas, al terninations ending in i, u or e and preceded by na, or whatever nunber they nay be, wil be pragrihya. as a nater or ract, there are only two such terninations satisrying the above conditions nanely ani and anu. The rule nay thererore be put in the rolowing words or Dr. nal nuler:- "The terninations or ani and anu non. plur. nasc. and non. dual or the pronoun adas are pragrihya." as ani asva "Those horses", and anu asate. There is no elanple or the word adas ending in e. Why do we say "or the word adas"? The leters i, u, e rolowing arter the n or any other word wil not be pragrihya. as sani+atra = sanyatra "this sani tre." Why do we say "arter the leter n"? Because in the elanple anuke+atra = anuketra, "those here," the e, preceded not by n but by the ka or akac [5.3.71] is not pragrihya, which it would have ben by the inrluence or sūtra i, which includes e as wel as i and u, and ron which the word dual is not suplied here, else this rule would be useles.
ck: the sane leters arter the n or the pronoun atas are prakrhya in the pronoun atas, the tual ternination in i, u or e til pe prakrihya py rorce or the last sūtra, put the present sûtra nakes this atition, that in the case or atas, al terninations entink in i, u or e ant precetet py na, or thatever nunper they nay pe, til pe prakrihya. as a nater or ract, there are only to such terninations satisryink the apove contitions nanely ani ant anu. the rule nay thererore pe put in the rolotink torts or tr. nal nuler:- "the terninations or ani ant anu non. plur. nasc. ant non. tual or the pronoun atas are prakrihya." as ani asva "those horses", ant anu asate. there is no elanple or the tort atas entink in e. thy to te say "or the tort atas"? the leters i, u, e rolotink arter the n or any other tort til not pe prakrihya. as sani+atra = sanyatra "this sani tre." thy to te say "arter the leter n"? pecause in the elanple anuke+atra = anuketra, "those here," the e, precetet not py n put py the ka or akac [5.3.71] is not prakrihya, thich it toult have pen py the inrluence or sūtra i, thich inclutes e as tel as i ant u, ant ron thich the tort tual is not supliet here, else this rule toult pe useles.
s: The same letters after the म् of the pronoun अदस् are प्रगृह्य In the pronoun अदस्, the dual termination in ई, ऊ or ए will be pragrihya by force of the last sūtra, but the present sûtra makes this addition, that in the case of अदस्, all terminations ending in ई, ऊ or ए and preceded by म, of whatever number they may be, will be pragrihya. As a matter of fact, there are only two such terminations satisfying the above conditions namely अमी and अमू. The rule may therefore be put in the following words of Dr. Max Muller:- "The terminations of अमी and अमू nom. plur. masc. and nom. dual of the pronoun अदस् are pragrihya." As अमी अश्वाः "Those horses", and अमू आसते. There is no example of the word adas ending in ए. Why do we say "of the word adas"? The letters ई, ऊ, ए following after the म् of any other word will not be pragrihya. As शमी+अत्र = शम्यत्र "this sami tree." Why do we say "after the letter म्"? Because in the example अमुके+अत्र = अमुकेऽत्र, "those here," the ए, preceded not by म् but by the क of अकच् [[5.3.71]] is not pragrihya, which it would have been by the influence of sūtra II, which includes ए as well as ई and ऊ, and from which the word dual is not supplied here, else this rule would be useless.

pk: The aril se (the Vedic substitute or the case-ariles) is a pragrhya in the Vedic sanskrit, the declension or nouns sonetines dirers sonewhat ron the ordinary sanskrit. One or the peculiar Vedic terninations, which replace the ordinary declensional terninations is caled se [7.1.39]. Thus asneindrabrhaspati. Or this substitute se, the initial sa is indicatory, the real suril being e. This rinal e is a pragrihya. in the sacred literature there is only one elanple or this pragrihya, as given above; while in initation or this, we have in secular writing phrases as, tveiti, yusne iti, ne iti &c.

One or the peculiar Vetic terninations, thich replace the ortinary teclensional terninations is calet se [7.1.39]. thus asneintraprhaspati. Or this supstitute se, the initial sa is inticatory, the real suril peink e. this rinal e is a prakrihya. in the sacret literature there is only one elanple or this prakrihya, as kiven apove; thile in initation or this, te have in secular tritink phrases as, tveiti, yusne iti, ne iti &c.
s: The affix शे (the Vedic substitute of the case-affixes) is a प्रगृह्य In the Vedic Sanskrit, the declension of nouns sometimes differs somewhat from the ordinary Sanskrit. One of the peculiar Vedic terminations, which replace the ordinary declensional terminations is called शे [[7.1.39]]. Thus अस्मेइन्द्राबृहस्पती. Of this substitute शे, the initial श is indicatory, the real suffix being ए. This final ए is a pragrihya. In the sacred literature there is only one example of this pragrihya, as given above; while in imitation of this, we have in secular writing phrases as, त्वेइति, युष्मे इति, मे इति &c.

s: A particle [[1.4.56]] consisting of a single vowel, with the exception of the particle आङ् is प्रगृह्य This sūtra consists of three words: निपातः "particle", एकाच् "consisting of one vowel," अनाङ् "with the exception of आङ्." All such particles technically called nipäta [[1.4.56]] which consist of a simple vowel without any consonant, are pragřihya and therefore are not liable to the rules of sandhi. As इ इन्द्र "Oh, Indra" उ उत्तिष्ठ "O arise." It follows from the above definition that those nipätas which consist of two or more letters, vowel and consonant, are not pragrihya, e. g. प्र in प्राग्नये वाचमीरय. आङ् which is not a pragrihya, has four significations:- As a diminutive particle when joined to adjectives and nouns, as आ+उष्णम् = ओष्णम् "little hot, tepid" (2) as a prefix to verbs, it expresses the senses of "near" "nearto," and with verbs of "motion," "taking" &c., it shows the reverse of the action, as गम् 'to go', आगम 'to come;' आ+इहि = एहि, (3) as showing the limit inceptive (अभिविधि) "from," "ever since," as आजन्मनः "ever since his birth," (4) as showing the limit exclusive (मर्यादा), "till" "until" as आ+अध्ययनात् = आध्ययनात्, "until the reading begins." When the particle आ has not any one of the above four senses and is used in expressing regret &c., it is a pragrihya, as आ एवं किलासीत् "Ah! such there once was", आ एवं मन्यसे "Oh! do you think so." The word एकाच् in this aphorism has a peculiar meaning. It means "consisting of one vowel and nothing else." In other words, the vowels themselves when used as निपात, e. g. आ, उ, इ &c. But the term एकाच् has a wider signification than that given to it in this sūtra. It means "a word or a portion of a word consisting of one vowel which can be pronounced at once"- in other words एकाच् means a "syllable". In that sense the words प्र, नि, वि &c., will also be एकाच्, but not so here. Therefore the rule of sandhi will apply to them, thus प्राग्नये वाचमीरय. See sūtra [[6.1.1]] where the word एकाच् means a monosyllable. Why do we say "a nipata?" Because if the single vowel is not a particle, but something else, an affix &c., then it will not be a pragrihya, as the final अ in चकार "he did", is the affix of third person perfect tense, and is liable to sandhi; as चकारात्र.

pk: The rinal o or a vocative singular [2.3.49] berore the word iti acording to sakalya , in a secular or non-vedic literature is a pragrhya This sūtra gives the opinion or the nishi sakalya, so that it is an optional rule. Thus both rorns vayaviti (rorned acording to the general rule or sandhi) and vayo iti (where o is pragrihya) are corect. in ârsha literature the sandhi is inperative, not optional, as eta ga brahnabanDavityabravit. The nention or the nane or any sage, such as that or sakalya in this sūtra, serves generaly one or the two purposes :- (1) either it nakes the rule an optional one, vibhåsharthan, or (2) the nention is nerely ror the sake or showing respect to the particular sage, the rule would have stod as wel without such nention; pujárthan, as the word Kåsyapa in sutra [1.2.15].

s: The final ओ of a vocative singular [[2.3.49]] before the word इति according to शाकल्य , in a secular or non-vedic literature is a प्रगृह्य This sūtra gives the opinion of the Rishi Sakalya, so that it is an optional rule. Thus both forms वायविति (formed according to the general rule of sandhi) and वायो इति (where ओ is pragrihya) are correct. In ârsha literature the sandhi is imperative, not optional, as एता गा ब्रह्मबन्धवित्यब्रवीत्. The mention of the name of any sage, such as that of Sakalya in this sūtra, serves generally one of the two purposes :- (1) either it makes the rule an optional one, vibhåshartham, or (2) the mention is merely for the sake of showing respect to the particular sage, the rule would have stood as well without such mention; pujártham, as the word Kåsyapa in sutra [[1.2.15]].

Let us take the elanple where a case-aril is changed into a leter honogeneous with the prior. Thus the case-aril or the seventh case is ni (i). in rorning the 7.s. or tanu "body," we have tanu+i. The i wil be changed into a honogeneous leter with u and we have tanu+u=tanu "in the body," as, aDyasyan nanakitanu (ror nanakyan tanvan). This is the Vedic rorn, the secular rorn being tanvan. sinilarly gOri+i = gOri "on the Gauri," as sono gOri aDisrita (nig Veda il.12.3). it is in such cases, thererore, that the long ī and ū are used in the sense or locative, and are pragrihya. it is only long ī and ū which are pragrihya, and not any other vowel, though used in the sense or locative. Thus by the sane aphorisn (Vi.i.39) ḍå (â) nay be enployed to denote the seventh case-aril.
